title: Chapter 2
content:
The line of people waiting outside the churchyard soup kitchen stretched down the block with no end in sight. The moment a spot at one of the blue plastic picnic tables cleared, another crowd swooped in to fill it.

Framing the scene through his viewfinder, Journalist Yoon scanned the courtyard until his lens caught one of the volunteers.

Even from a distance, the guy in the green apron stood out. He was tall, built like a brick wall, and had the kind of movie-star good looks that immediately drew the eye. To top it off, he was effortlessly charming, flashing easy, disarming smiles at every person who walked by.

"Damn. Look at him," Yoon muttered.

Sitting beside him with an ice cream bar between his teeth, Senior Journalist Kwak turned his head to glance over. "Kang Il-hyun?"

"Who'd ever guess that guy's a mobster?" Yoon said, adjusting his focus. "If you only judged a book by its cover, you’d think he was a A-list actor."

"Yeah, well, the difference between him and an actor," Kwak rasped, "is that he actually chops people up."

Yoon pulled his eye away from the camera and shot a look at his senior. "Wait, you’ve seen him do it?"

"Do I need to see it with my own eyes?" Kwak snorted. "They call themselves a 'corporation,' but everyone and their mother knows it’s a syndicate front. You remember that congressman who turned up dead—supposedly a suicide—three years ago? That was all—"

"Hard at work, gentlemen?"

A man materialized out of thin air between them, interrupting their hushed gossiping to hand over two ice-cold bottles of energy drink. He was grinning as wide as he could, but the intense, razor-sharp aura radiating off him told a completely different story. Faint, jagged scars lined the back of his hands—battle marks that time hadn't managed to erase.

"We’d really appreciate a favorable piece," the man said, locking eyes with Kwak and leaning heavily on his next words. "As you can see... our organization does a lot of good for the community."

Kwak swallowed hard, taking the two bottles with a nervous, practiced grin. He recognized the guy immediately: he was Kang Il-hyun’s personal secretary—which, in mob speak, made him the second-in-command of the entire operation.

What was his name again...? Park Tae-soo?

Tae-soo offered a polite nod, gave them a slight bow, and slipped back into the crowd.

Kwak immediately leaned in close, dropping his voice to a whisper. "Hey... you don’t think he heard us, do you?"

"Even if he did, so what?" Yoon shrugged. "It's not like you were lying."

Kwak instinctively wiped a bead of sweat from his forehead. "Is... is this sweat? Did I look nervous? Was it obvious?"

"Why are you losing your cool?" Yoon chuckled. "It's not like he's gonna put a hit out on you right here."

At the word hit, Kwak stared down suspiciously at the bottle in his hand. Tossing it out felt like a quick way to draw unwanted attention, but drinking it gave him the creeps. While he was agonizing over it, Yoon casually popped his cap and chugged the entire thing down. Kwak reached out to stop him, but it was already too late.

"You idiot! Why did you drink that?!" Kwak hissed. "You don't know what they put in there!"

Yoon merely flicked his chin toward the food line.

Tae-soo was now standing beside Kang Il-hyun, whispering something into his ear. Il-hyun’s eyes slowly shifted across the yard, landing straight on the two journalists.

Spooked out of his mind, Kwak immediately turned his back to them, muttering under his breath, "Dammit... why is he staring over here?"

"Who knows? Beats me," Yoon said. Raising his bottle, he gave Il-hyun a small, grateful nod.

Il-hyun offered a polite, gentle smile in return, bowed his head respectfully, and went right back to scooping food for the line. The way he made eye contact with every single homeless person, smiling warmly and even shaking hands when someone reached out, made him look less like a gangster and more like a politician running for office.

"Fucking disgusting."

Kang Tae-han ripped off his glasses, squirted a generous dollop of hand sanitizer into his palm, and aggressively rubbed his hands together. He’d been handing out rice to those bums, and they kept grabbing at his hands to thank him. He’d already scrubbed them with soap and water, but he still couldn't shake the filth.

"Cockroaches, the lot of them," he spat onto the pavement, pulling a cigarette from his pocket. "Offer them a free meal and they swarm like vermin."

A lieutenant instantly stepped forward, flicking open a lighter to spark the tip. Tae-han took a deep drag and exhaled a thick cloud into the stifling air.

Even though it was only May, the heat felt like a furnace. The news anchors had been droning on about how this summer was going to see a record-breaking heatwave, but thinking back, they ran that exact same segment every damn year.

A short distance away, his younger brother, Kang Il-hyun, was posing for photos with the other volunteers. Watching him put on that righteous, saintly act made a sneer curdle on Tae-han's lips. Hypocritical bastard.

Finished with the photo-op, Il-hyun thanked the volunteers, unloosed his green apron, and tossed it to a nearby subordinate. After exchanging a few brief words, he started walking over to where Tae-han was standing.

At nearly six-foot-three with broad shoulders and a lean, athletic frame, Il-hyun naturally commanded the attention of every eye in the yard. His dress shirt sleeves were rolled up, exposing thick, corded forearms that flexed with every stride. No wonder women throw themselves at him, drooling to get a piece, Tae-han thought bitterly. Arrogant prick.

Stopping beside him, Il-hyun cracked open a bottle of water and chugged it down.

"Look at you, playing the saint," Tae-han sneered. "You missed your calling, brother. Should’ve been an actor."

Il-hyun tossed the empty plastic bottle cleanly into a trash can, his tone dropping an octave—cool, low, and laced with quiet authority.

"Instead of running your mouth, keep a tighter leash on our men. A reporter was just snooping around."

"A reporter? Who?"

Il-hyun pulled out a cigarette, lit it, and looked down at his brother with an unreadable glaze in his eyes.

With his wire-rimmed glasses and constant furrowed brow, Tae-han was the spitting image of his mother over in the States—always anxious, always high-strung. Il-hyun deliberately blew a plume of gray smoke straight into his face, watching the wrinkle between Tae-han's brows dig even deeper.

Tae-han swatted the smoke away, cursing under his breath. "And do me a favor—try smiling more in public. It’s not gonna kill you."

"Smiling is your department," Il-hyun said smoothly. "Feel free to do enough for the both of us."

He flicked his cigarette away, the glowing ember cutting through the air. "Forget it. Working with you is like trying to clap with one hand."

Tae-han's eyes flashed with anger. Even if they had different mothers, the fact that a brother eight years his junior talked down to him like a subordinate cut deep. When they were younger, Tae-han would just pin him down and beat some sense into him, but ever since Il-hyun had his growth spurt, that was off the table.

When was the last time he’d laid a hand on him? Middle school, maybe? They’d gotten into an argument over something stupid, and Tae-han had lost his temper, kicking the kid ruthlessly while he was on the ground.

Except that day hadn't ended like the others.

Bleeding on the floor, Il-hyun had snatched a paring knife from the housekeeper’s tray and shoved it straight into Tae-han’s side, sending him straight to the ER.

Tae-han still remembered that moment with terrifying clarity. Il-hyun had been smiling.

“Hit me again,” the kid had whispered, “and the next one goes in your heart.”

They were mobsters in name, but Tae-han and his brothers had grown up with clean hands. They’d spent their lives gorging themselves on the rich empire their father, Chairman Kang, had built—drinking, partying, enjoying the high life without ever having to bleed for it or worry about getting crushed by someone bigger.

Il-hyun, though... Il-hyun was built different. Despite sharing the same upbringing, he had an insatiable appetite for blood, growing more vicious and cunning by the day. He picked fights left and right, yet his execution was always so flawless that Chairman Kang never had a reason to bench him. And that grated on Tae-han most of all.

As Tae-han brooded over the past, his wife, Park Sun-joo, finished saying her goodbyes to the volunteers and walked over with measured, elegant steps. Seeing her neat hair and toned-down makeup, Tae-han snorted softly. Look at that. Another actor in the family.

"You worked so hard today, dear," she said softly, before turning to her brother-in-law. "You as well, Il-hyun."

"Nonsense, Sister. You're the one who pulled the heavy weight," Il-hyun replied smoothly. "You look radiant today."

Sun-joo covered her mouth with a delicate flutter, giggling at the compliment. Tae-han rolled his eyes at the display. Disgusting. His wife shot him a cold glare, but he simply looked away, ignoring her completely.

Just then, Park Tae-soo approached them with a cell phone in his hand, his posture tense.

"Executive Director," Tae-soo whispered carefully. "You need to take this."

Il-hyun took the phone. As he listened to the voice on the line, a sudden, murderous chill flickered in his eyes before vanishing just as quickly.

"I'm on my way. Tell everyone to keep their mouths shut," Il-hyun commanded, handing the phone back to Tae-soo. "Get the car ready. We're leaving now."

As Tae-soo hurried off, Tae-han’s curiosity got the better of him. "Where are you going?"

Il-hyun let out a dry, frigid laugh. "Our little brother messed up. Big time."

"Ah, that fucking brat," Tae-han spat, not needing to hear another word.

They had a half-brother—a twenty-something hedonist who was the undisputed black sheep of the family. He spent his days buried in nightlife and had recently gotten hooked on drugs, leaving a trail of messes wherever he went.

"I'll take my leave first, Sister," Il-hyun said with a polite bow. "I'll see you both at tomorrow's dinner. Get home safely."

Turning on his heel, Il-hyun walked toward his sedan parked in the rear courtyard. The warm, approachable demeanor he'd worn all afternoon dissolved instantly, replaced by a mask of sheer, icy violence.

Tae-soo held the rear door open, then quickly slid into the driver’s seat.

"Casualties?" Il-hyun asked coldly as the engine hummed to life.

"Six minor injuries, one in a coma," Tae-soo reported. "A fight broke out before the knives came out. Fortunately, Representative Seo’s son only sustained light scratches."

Il-hyun let out a low curse, staring out the window. "Call Representative Seo. Tell him I’ll pay him a personal visit tonight."
